# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user acts on; neither is ever sent by itself. A prompt card has buttons that send it to Code, Chain, or Spec, whichever mode it names, and one that puts it in the chat input to edit first.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.

36-A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started, and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.
37-Each background task is known by its kind, from what started it: a subagent, started by an Agent or Task tool call, or a command, a shell command run in the background. Its start is when the harness said it had started, so how long it has been running can be told. A single background task can be stopped while the run goes on, without ending the run or any other task: the harness is asked, on the run's input, to stop that task by its id, Claude Code with its stream-json control request for stopping a task. The task then ends when the harness notifies its end, as ever, as stopped, and the harness carries on with what came of it. Stopping one is never done by stopping the harness's process, and a run whose input is already closed, or whose harness can't be fed, can't stop one on its own.
38:A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the state of that last result, unless its reply's verdict says it failed, when it finishes Failed, as the failures say; until the process exits, the task keeps running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the background, since its whole process group is ended with it.
39-A background command that never ends on its own, as a dev server started with `npm run dev`, `vite`, or `node server.js`, or a watcher, never keeps a task running once its work is done. Once a result has come, every message sent has been taken in, and no subagent is still going, a background command still running holds the run open only while it is busy: one that has printed nothing for 60 seconds since that result, as a server does once it has started and waits for requests, is taken as idle. ## Suspense Fluency

The Suspense fluency is how Suspense works, as a harness working in any project needs to know it to talk about it or write for it: what the modes are and what each may change, how a Chain prompt runs, how prompts and questions are handed back to the user, and what the application adds to a prompt of its own accord. Every mode but Freeform is pointed at it, so a question asked to write a Chain prompt, or a task asked about the queue, knows what that is, in a project that says nothing of Suspense itself. Like the Piton fluency, it is never part of the system prompt, so the prompt cache holds whatever the mode.
It is the same for every project, and is the application's own, not a project's to edit: its source is a Markdown file in this application's own repository, `suspense-fluency.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, baked into the application when it is built, as they are, so a build always ships with whatever it says, and a build can't be made without it. It is not among the prompts a project saves or the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window) edits.
It is written to the Suspense fluency file, `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, before any Code, Chain, Spec, or Ask prompt is compiled, whenever the file isn't there or doesn't hold what the application ships, so it keeps in step with the application rather than the project. It is written as text, never read as Piton, holds no placeholder and no path of the machine it was written on, and so reads the same on any machine.
It says, plainly and briefly, written for a harness rather than for the user, each of these in a short paragraph of its own.
- that Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code, and that a prompt is sent to the harness in one of five modes, in the order and with the meanings the PromptModes gives: Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is, Chain changes the spec and then the code to match, Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is, Ask asks a question and changes nothing, and Freeform passes a prompt to the harness exactly as typed
- that Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks, run in a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each, queueing behind tasks of their own lane, and that questions run at once and never queue
- that a Chain prompt runs as two steps: a spec step, which writes the prompt into the spec, then a code step, sent the prompt and what the spec step replied, which changes the code to match the spec as built, and that each step is its own run, in its own lane
- that Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, and the spec's references and the understanding file with them, so a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms, and never holds a <task-instructions> block, steps the mode already takes, or instructions about building, checking, the understanding file, or the verdict line a task ends its reply with
- how to write a good prompt for each mode: a Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec; a Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the spec it follows; an Ask prompt is a question; and a prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference under the harness's directory, as the user would
- that an answer hands a prompt back to the user, for them to read, edit, and send, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, and asks the user something back as one whose info string is `suspense-question`, with any answers to pick from one per line, each starting with `- `, as the card format says, both shown as cards the user acts on, a prompt card with buttons that send it to Code, Chain, or Spec, never sent by themselves
- what a task's understanding file is, the short list of constraints it takes from the spec, shown beside the task as it runs
- that the user can cancel, resend, or send a task to the other mode, send more to a running task, and start a new conversation, so a prompt never needs to say any of that is possible
It names no project, location, harness, or file of any one project, and says nothing a mode's own instructions already tell a run that sees them, such as how the spec is read or written.
SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask instructions each say, on a paragraph of its own, to read that file once in the conversation when the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or calls for writing a prompt or a question for the user, before doing so. A Chain prompt's code step is pointed at it through the Code instructions, and a Code task sent to Spec through the Spec instructions. Freeform sends no instructions, and is never pointed at it. Where the file can't be written, SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the paragraph pointing at it is left out.

## Spec Reading

The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own, saved with its data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, in spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window); with no file yet the project uses its default.

## Code To Spec

The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, after the Spec instructions. It may use every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the templates, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window); with no file yet the project uses its default.
The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

## Card Format

Every question is told how an answer hands back prompts and questions in the forms the [AskConversation](../ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation) shows as cards, so whenever the user asks for a prompt, it comes back as a card they can send to Code, Chain, or Spec. It is not a project's to edit or leave out: the application adds it to each question's <task-instructions> block, after the project's Ask instructions, on a paragraph of its own, whatever those say, including a project's Ask instructions saved before it was added, which are kept as they are. Its text is baked into the application from this application's own repository, in `ask-cards.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, and a build can't be made without it. It is never given to a task, and Freeform sends nothing. It says:
Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.

- that Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code, and that a prompt is sent to the harness in one of five modes, in the order and with the meanings the PromptModes gives: Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is, Chain changes the spec and then the code to match, Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is, Ask asks a question and changes nothing, and Freeform passes a prompt to the harness exactly as typed
- that Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks, run in a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each, queueing behind tasks of their own lane, and that questions run at once and never queue
- that a Chain prompt runs as two steps: a spec step, which writes the prompt into the spec, then a code step, sent the prompt and what the spec step replied, which changes the code to match the spec as built, and that each step is its own run, in its own lane

- that the user can cancel, resend, or send a task to the other mode, send more to a running task, and start a new conversation, so a prompt never needs to say any of that is possible

## Spec Reading

The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own, saved with its data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, in spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window); with no file yet the project uses its default.

## Code To Spec

The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, after the Spec instructions. It may use every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the templates, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window); with no file yet the project uses its default.
The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

## Card Format

Every question is told how an answer hands back prompts and questions in the forms the [AskConversation](../ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation) shows as cards, so whenever the user asks for a prompt, it comes back as a card they can send to Code, Chain, or Spec. Its text is baked into the application from this application's own repository, in `ask-cards.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, and a build can't be made without it. It is never given to a task, and Freeform sends nothing. It says:
Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. After your reply, end with one line of its own that is exactly `SUSPENSE-VERDICT: done` if you did the work this prompt asks for, or exactly `SUSPENSE-VERDICT: failed` if you couldn't: if you failed, couldn't write or change what you were to, were blocked by the sandbox, a missing file, or anything else, or gave up. The code bakes it in through `system_prompts::task_verdict()`. For the same reason, the shipped `.suspense/system-prompts/suspense-fluency.md` still doesn't say that prompts never include the verdict line. That sentence needs adding by hand.

**What changed:**
- **The request:** Code, Chain and Spec tasks, including a chain's code step and a Code task sent to Spec, now get the verdict request last in their instructions. Questions, resume messages and Freeform don't (`src/hidden_anchor.rs`).
- **Reading it:** the app reads only the last non-blank line of the last result's reply, trimmed and ignoring case. It takes that line out of the reply, so it is never shown or handed to the next step (`src/task_table.rs`).
- **Failing the task:** if the line says failed, the task is marked Failed and its reply appears under the heading "The run reported that it couldn't do the work." (`src/prompt_mode.rs`).
- **After a restart:** the history replays the run's saved output, so the task still reads Failed.
- **Downstream:** chains and Planning already handle Failed tasks, so they follow without further changes.

**Testing:** I couldn't build in place. The other baked prompts and the project config can't be read from here either, so I type-checked and tested a copy of the crate using placeholder prompt files. The Chain's spec step didn't write this request into the spec. What it handed on as its output is my reply from the previous task, the verdict line, not a description of this change. Building it from the prompt alone would be the workaround the instructions rule out. I'd run the spec step again first, for example with this:

```suspense-prompt spec
When a task's verdict was misread, the user can overrule it after the task has ended. A task that failed because of its verdict shows "Mark as done" beside the reason it failed. A task whose verdict said done shows "Mark as failed" in the menu of its output. Either choice sets the task's status (.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) and saves it in the task's history record, so it still holds after a restart. The status tooltip says the outcome was set by hand. A chain stopped by the overruled step offers to send the steps it didn't run. In Planning, a story whose task is overruled to Done goes to Done when the sprint is closed, and one overruled to Failed goes back to Next sprint (.claude/reference/scope/planning/index.md#planning). Only a task that has ended can be overruled. A task that failed to compile or run, or that the harness reported as an error, offers neither choice.
```

Once the spec has been built with that in it, sending the same prompt to Code will implement it against the spec.
